item.title: Oil eases as traders assess supply risks from US-Iran tensions
item.description:
Oil prices eased slightly on Tuesday as traders weighed the potential for supply disruptions after the United States issued fresh guidance for commercial vessels navigating the Strait of Hormuz, maintaining attention on simmering tensions between Washington and Tehran over Iran's nuclear program.

Brent crude futures and West Texas Intermediate both fell by roughly 0.4% in early trading, according to Reuters. The modest pullback followed a more than 1% rise on Monday when the U.S. Department of Transportation's Maritime Administration released the new shipping advisory.

item.title: Honda's quarterly operating profit drops 61% on tariffs, EV woes
item.description:
Honda Motor reported a 42 percent drop in nine-month net profit on Tuesday, as the Japanese automaker continued to struggle under the weight of U.S. import tariffs, weakening electric vehicle demand, and ongoing chip supply disruptions.

Net profit for the nine months ended December fell to 465.44 billion yen ($2.99 billion), down from 805.26 billion yen in the same period a year earlier, according to the company's earnings report. Nine-month revenue declined 2.2 percent to 15.976 trillion yen.

item.title: January 2026 ranks fifth-warmest on record despite polar extremes
item.description:
Europe recorded its coldest January since 2010 as polar vortex disruptions sent Arctic air flooding across the continent, while the Southern Hemisphere simultaneously endured deadly heatwaves and wildfires, according to new data from the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service released Tuesday.

Despite the sharp regional contrasts, global temperatures remained near record levels. January 2026 was the fifth-warmest January on record, with a global average surface temperature of 12.95 degrees Celsius—just 0.28 degrees Celsius cooler than January 2025, the warmest January ever recorded.

item.title: Satellite data reveals faster methane breakdown in stratosphere
item.description:
University of Washington researchers have produced the first satellite-based estimate of methane destruction in the stratosphere, finding that the powerful greenhouse gas breaks down at a higher rate than climate models previously predicted. The study, published Sunday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, offers new clarity on how methane accumulates in Earth's atmosphere—a long-standing puzzle for climate scientists.

The finding addresses a persistent gap between two methods of calculating global methane levels that have historically produced conflicting results. By replacing model-based estimates with satellite observations, the researchers brought the two approaches into close agreement for the first time.

item.title: Satellite images show Iran burying nuclear site entrances
item.description:
Satellite imagery captured this week shows that Iran has completely buried all three tunnel entrances at its Isfahan nuclear complex with soil, in a move that analysts say mirrors defensive preparations taken before American strikes devastated the facility last year.

The Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS) published high-resolution images taken Sunday showing the middle and southern tunnel entrances at the site are now "unrecognizable and fully covered in soil," while the northernmost entrance—which had already been fitted with additional defensive measures—has also been backfilled. No vehicle or personnel activity is visible around the entrances, according to the institute.

item.title: Yen extends gains as Takaichi's landslide win reshapes Japan markets
item.description:
The Japanese yen extended gains against the US dollar on Tuesday as markets digested Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's historic election victory, while the greenback remained under pressure ahead of key American economic releases this week.

The USD/JPY pair fell to around 155.50 on Tuesday morning, continuing a slide that began after the ruling Liberal Democratic Party secured a supermajority in Sunday's snap election. The yen's appreciation marked a reversal of the pre-election trend that had pushed the currency toward the closely watched 160 level against the dollar.

item.title: Study: Climate change could halve global grazing land by 2100
item.description:
Up to half of the world's grasslands suitable for cattle, sheep, and goat farming could become unviable by the end of the century due to rising global temperatures, according to a major new study that warns of severe consequences for more than 100 million pastoralists and up to 1.6 billion livestock worldwide.

The research, published in the journal PNAS on February 9, was led by scientists at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany. It identifies a "safe climatic space" for grazing systems that cover roughly one-third of Earth's land surface and represent the world's largest food production system.

item.title: Study finds half of world's coral reefs bleached in 2014-17
item.description:
More than half of the world's coral reefs were bleached during a prolonged marine heatwave from 2014 to 2017, according to a study published Tuesday in the journal Nature Communications. The research represents the first comprehensive global analysis of what scientists have named the Third Global Bleaching Event, confirming it as the most severe coral die-off ever recorded.

The international team of researchers estimated that 51 percent of the world's reef areas suffered moderate or greater bleaching during the three-year period, with 15 percent experiencing substantial mortality. The findings paint a grim picture that scientists warn is already being surpassed by an ongoing fourth global bleaching event.

item.title: Europe's Ariane 64 rocket to make maiden launch Thursday
item.description:
Europe's most powerful rocket is poised to make history. On Thursday, the Ariane 64 rocket will lift off from the European spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana, marking the first flight of the four-booster configuration and carrying 32 satellites for Amazon Leo's broadband internet constellation.

The mission, designated VA267 by Arianespace, will open a launch window at 4:45 p.m. UTC, with the window closing at 5:13 p.m. UTC. The flight represents the first in a series of 18 missions contracted by Amazon to deploy its low Earth orbit satellite network, designed to compete with SpaceX's Starlink service.

item.title: Macron insists €100B European fighter jet program is 'not dead'
item.description:
French President Emmanuel Macron defended Europe's troubled Future Combat Air System on Monday, telling Le Monde and the Financial Times that the €100 billion fighter jet program is "not dead," even as multiple officials in Paris and Berlin have declared it on the brink of collapse.

The assertion comes amid mounting pessimism about the joint French-German-Spanish initiative, which Macron personally launched with former German Chancellor Angela Merkel in 2017 to develop a sixth-generation fighter jet, drones, and a shared combat cloud to replace the aging Rafale and Eurofighter fleets by 2040.

item.title: Russia says peace deal impossible without its own security guarantees
item.description:
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko declared on Tuesday that any peace settlement in Ukraine must include security guarantees for Moscow, describing such assurances as a fundamental condition for ending the nearly four-year conflict.

"We recognise that a peace settlement in Ukraine must take account of Ukraine's security interests, but a key factor, of course, is Russia's security interests," Grushko told the Russian outlet Izvestia on February 10. "If you look carefully and study the statements made by the leaders of the European Union, no one talks about security guarantees for Russia. This is a key element of a peace accord. Without it, an agreement is impossible."

item.title: Astronomers report possible pulsar near Milky Way's black hole
item.description:
Astronomers may have detected a millisecond pulsar in the innermost region of the Milky Way's Galactic Center, a finding that could provide an unprecedented tool for testing Einstein's theory of General Relativity if confirmed. The discovery, announced Monday in a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal, represents one of the most sensitive pulsar searches ever conducted toward the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*.

A research team led by Karen Perez, a recent Columbia University PhD graduate, used the Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope in West Virginia as part of the Breakthrough Listen initiative to conduct more than 20 hours of observations targeting the galactic center. The survey included 11 hours focused on the innermost 1.4 arcminutes of the region between May 2021 and December 2023.

item.title: NASA taps Infleqtion to fly first quantum gravity sensor to space
item.description:
NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory has selected quantum technology company Infleqtion to collaborate on a mission that will deploy the world's first quantum gravity sensor in orbit. The Quantum Gravity Gradiometer Pathfinder (QGGPf) mission, backed by more than $20 million in contracted funding, is expected to launch in 2030 for a one-year demonstration in low Earth orbit.

The announcement, made Monday, marks a major step forward in U.S. leadership in space-based quantum sensing. The satellite mission will test technologies designed to measure subtle variations in Earth's gravitational field, monitoring mass dynamics across the planet's surface including changes in water, ice, and land resources.

item.title: Study finds Earth's core may hold 45 oceans' worth of hydrogen
item.description:
A new study has found that Earth's core could contain up to 45 times more hydrogen than all the planet's oceans combined, a discovery that reshapes understanding of where our world's water came from. The research, published in Nature Communications, suggests that most of Earth's water has been with the planet since its formation approximately 4.5 billion years ago rather than being delivered later by comets and asteroids.

"It really changes the way we think of where our water comes from," said Hilke Schlichting, a professor of Earth, planetary and space science at the University of California, Los Angeles, who was not involved in the study.

item.title: China's Einstein Probe captures first likely black hole-white dwarf collision
item.description:
China's Einstein Probe space telescope has detected what scientists believe to be the first direct observation of an intermediate-mass black hole tearing apart and consuming a white dwarf star, according to a study published this month in Science Bulletin.

The extraordinary cosmic event, designated EP250702a, was detected on July 2, 2025, during a routine sky survey. Scientists discovered that X-ray emissions from the source appeared nearly 24 hours before NASA's Fermi satellite recorded associated gamma-ray bursts—a sequence that immediately distinguished it from ordinary cosmic explosions.

item.title: Police, protesters clash in Sydney as Israeli president’s visit sparks unrest
item.description:
Police and protesters clashed violently in central Sydney on Monday evening during demonstrations against Israeli President Isaac Herzog's visit to Australia, with 27 people arrested and at least nine facing criminal charges, including allegations of assaulting officers.

Approximately 6,000 people gathered at Sydney's Town Hall for what organizers, the Palestine Action Group, described as a peaceful rally opposing Herzog's four-day trip to Australia. As speeches concluded, demonstrators expressed their intention to march toward the NSW Parliament, defying protest restrictions that had been imposed under emergency powers following December's Bondi Beach terror attack.

item.title: Data center electricity demand to triple by 2035, new study finds
item.description:
The world's data centers are poised to consume roughly three times their current electricity by 2035, driven by the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud computing, according to new industry projections. Renewable energy and nuclear power are expected to supply the majority of this increased demand, even as grid infrastructure struggles to keep pace.

A report from Precedence Research published this week projects that global data center electricity consumption will climb from approximately 460 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2024 to more than 1,300 TWh by 2035. BloombergNEF's December 2025 forecast similarly estimated that U.S. data center power demand alone will reach 106 gigawatts by 2035, up from 40 gigawatts today—a nearly threefold increase.

item.title: Carney says call with Trump on Gordie Howe Bridge was 'positive'
item.description:
Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke with President Donald Trump on Tuesday morning about the Gordie Howe International Bridge after Trump threatened to block its opening, describing the conversation as "positive" and expressing optimism the matter would be resolved.

The call came after Trump declared on his Truth Social platform Monday evening that he would "not permit" the bridge linking Windsor, Ontario, to Detroit, Michigan, to open until the United States is "fully compensated for everything we have given" Canada. Trump also demanded the U.S. receive ownership of "at least one half of this asset."

item.title: Trump considers second carrier if Iran talks fail
item.description:
The United States and Iran held their first nuclear negotiations since the 12-day war in June 2025, meeting indirectly in Muscat, Oman on February 6 with Omani officials serving as intermediaries. The talks mark a potential thaw after months of heightened tensions, though major disputes over uranium enrichment remain unresolved.

President Donald Trump described the discussions as "very good" and committed to further rounds of talks, while Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called them "a good start," despite acknowledging that significant work remains to establish trust between the two nations. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei characterized the half-day meeting as "a way to measure the seriousness of the other side" and to determine how the process could continue.

item.title: Pulsar discovery near Milky Way's center could test Einstein's relativity
item.description:
A flurry of findings from international research teams is prompting astronomers to reconsider long-held assumptions about the Milky Way's center and the nature of cosmic cataclysms observed by space telescopes.

A study published this week in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society proposes that the object at the heart of our galaxy may not be a supermassive black hole at all, but rather an ultra-dense clump of exotic dark matter. The research challenges the prevailing theory that Sagittarius A* — long believed to be a black hole with roughly 4 million times the mass of the Sun — is responsible for the extreme orbits of nearby stars racing at thousands of kilometers per second.
